en: Grasping his forelock, he could only kiss him;
“Farewell, Sarala,” he said, kissing him.
Your elder Bakai, the lion,
The swift steed Sarala,
Then drove him onto the road.
Your generous Manas, the leopard,
Leaning upon his battle-axe,
Was left lamenting his precious one.
His dear eyes like a saker's,
With each turn, tears flowed;
His dear eyes like currants,
Tears flowed a whip's length.
Your hero returned from entering Beijing,
Your hero was parted from his champions,
Had let all his people be slaughtered.
He took turmoil away from Beijing.
Karabayyr battle steeds,
With sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs—
Swift steeds he took from Beijing.
All the precious treasures,
He bundled and took from Beijing.
Gold and silver,
He loaded and took from Beijing.
Noble young wives and beautiful girls,
He plundered and took from Beijing.
He took red-tailed elephants;
He loaded gold upon elephants and took it;
He took a thousand dark-eyed women.
The most able warriors,
Those returning safely from Beijing,
The accomplished champions,
Took seven thousand horses each;
The lesser men who could not match them
Took seven hundred horses each.
All the exceptional ones
Drove six thousand horses each;
The lesser men who guarded their lives
Drove six hundred horses each.
All the mighty ones
Took girls in red dresses, slender-waisted,
Girls who moved with graceful swaying.
All the valued ones
Took skilled women with thimbles;
They took gold and jewels by the pood.
Opening the way for Islam,
Scattering the Chinese herds,
Plundering their goods,
Wreaking such destruction,
All their champions slaughtered,
Those left alive among the dead
Dispersed toward their destinations.
Those who dwelt in Sary-Arka,
Whom all the people who saw them
Called weighty, formidable warriors,
Who hulled their millet clean as stone,
Who praised their wives like maidens,
Parted from their Kökchö,
Turning toward Sary-Arka,
The Kazakhs took one road.
From their land called Crimea,
They too had come in their eagerness;
Struck from the flank,
Having lost their mighty khan Muzburchak,
Readying their red spears,
Girding on their swords without sheaths,
They too returned from entering Beijing,
Parted from their sovereign Muzburchak.
Their hero's head had been cut off;
Deceitful world, may you never prosper!
Their assembled troops came apart;
The Crimean people returned in one direction.
They were the Sary Nogoy people;
He was an extraordinary lord to his people.
At his feast a mare was slaughtered;
He was named hero Bokmurun,
The spring of the foothills,
Kökötöy's dear only child, born in his last years.
Clashing spears, breaking enemy ranks,
In the desert of It-Ölbös,
At Beijing of Kakan-Chin,
When the many Chinese came,
His appointed death too arrived: he fell to a bullet.
He had dwelt in broad Tashkent,
Was called a stately hero.
They too returned without ruling Beijing;
They were the Sary Nogoy people,
Parted from Bokmurun,
Loading gold upon camels:
“We have let Beijing take him,” they said;
They too suffered anguish for their khan,
Grieving and lamenting,
They too set out for their homeland.
Then Muzburchak and Khan Kökchö died,
So many fine souls died.
At that very Beijing,
Everyone who encountered it died.
As Manas stood grieving,
Between his back and neck,
The hero's wound began to ache,
The wound struck by a battle-axe.
Unable to mount his horse again,
Parted from his fierce champions,
Calamity fell upon Bakai.
Seated in mourning,
Khan Manas could not mount a horse.
Then Bakai pondered:
Pine is hard, willow soft;
He made a bier of juniper,
Laid a fine-cloth mattress beneath him,
Bound the sultan firmly upon it.
The anguish for Almambet,
The grief for Khan Syrgak,
Then the anguish for Khan Chubak—
Losing speech, his eyes darted wildly;
The hero hung limp, unable to speak.
Driving seven thousand red camels,
Then braiding the camels' tails,
Parted from their precious ones,
Thus the Muslim people suffered their anguish.
At Beijing the Holy One could not touch,
They turned back from their fighting.
The Muslims were left in mourning,
Oh hero, parted from their khans.
Dark night fell upon Khan Manas;
Then, turning back from Beijing,
Loading gold and spoils upon their steeds,
Parted from their falcons,
The hero set out toward Talas.
Having let Akkula fall to a bullet,
That was where Manas had lost him.
Saying, “I shall give a six-day respite,”
All the heroes,
Oh hero, that was where he had let them be struck down!
He had entered willingly and returned;
Your khan Manas, the leopard,
Then parted from his khans,
His ailing life wrung with pain.
“My devastating Almam!” he cried in grief;
Oh hero, at the thought his soul was scorched.
Upon his own once-prosperous head,
Oh hero, since grief had fallen,
His champion friend Bakai
Laid him snugly upon a bier.
Then blue-maned Manas—
The horse was just reaching its mature years—
Your hero he loaded upon Taybuurul.
Loading ammunition upon the swift camel,
That consummate leopard Bakai
Then set out toward Talas.
Without lying down to rest by day,
Without taking sleep at night,
Then they traveled by night toward Talas.
A deadly day had fallen upon his head;
Then trouble had fallen upon Manas.
So much gold, so many jewels,
He had won for the Muslims.
For six months, as khan in Beijing,
Noble Manas had stood;
Saying, “I shall call the azan aloud,”
He had let Kongurbay strike his head.
“If we arrive without warning,
It will destroy the people,” he said.
“The Argyn and the Kyrgyz
Will lose heart,” he said.
He provided six swift horses;
To the people of Talas,
Your hero sent a palm-sized letter:
“At Beijing no corsac fox could enter,
The leopard, Sultan Manas,
We have raised as khan,” it said.
“From Beijing that Solomon could not touch,
We have firmly taken dominion,” it said.
“The handsome, blue-maned lion Manas,
We have raised as khan of Beijing,” it said.
“With cotton belt and broad boots,
Kongurbay, khan of the monks,
We have bound to a leading rein,” it said.
“At Beijing that Solomon could not touch,
We have become the rulers,” it said.
“At Beijing Alexander could not tread,
Our endeavor has wholly prevailed;
Within it, your lord Alma,
We have raised as khan,” it said.
“The mountain of mined gold and tea,
We have taken as the Muslims' share,” it said.
“People dwelling in Talas,
Since we have captured Beijing,
Let them take heart and not die;
Let them slaughter a thousand black, white-blazed mares,
Slaughter a thousand dark camels,
Then let my people feast without stint.
Let my people gather at that feast;
The elders in their nineties,
Then the twelve-year-old boys,
Tell them to heed my words.
To that great feast where the people rejoice,
Let everyone come,” it said.
“Yrchy Uul, Yraman's son,
Stands singing beside him.
Tölgöchu, Döö Khan's son,
Casts his divination at his head.
My lord, Sultan Bakai,
Gives orders beside me.
Almambet's white royal tent,
With Aruuke dressed in finery,
Tell them to pitch at the mouth of Talas.
Before its door,
Of wholly barren gray mares,
Tell them to tether six.
Of tents made of gold,
Tell them to fold sixty.
Almambet's and Chubak's royal tents,
Tell them to pitch with doors adjoining in Talas.
The rosy-faced girls,
Tell them to wear bright red coats.
With ornamented braids and broad hips,
Then all the young wives,
Let them put on green headscarves.
The fully mature women,
Binding black bands around their heads,
For Almambet and Chubak,
Let them make ready their royal tents.
The worthy warriors,
Let them slaughter six mares each.
The helpless, poor and lowly,
Let them slaughter two mares each.”
Then he provided six swift horses,
Gave a letter for Kanykey in Talas.
To the Argyn and Kyrgyz in Talas,
After Yrchy Uul brought the news,
“We have captured Beijing,” he said.
After he arrived with this news,
The populace stirred with a roar,
The many people gathered together.
“Khan Manas is coming,” they said;
The people made preparations.
Having the news proclaimed firmly,
Your dear, fierce sister-in-law Kanykey took the lead;
Almambet's and Chubak's royal tents,
She had them brought without a moment's delay.
In the hollow of Zhylgynduu,
Along broad Talas,
Gathering much gold and wealth,
She had their doors pitched adjoining.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey,
A fine-cloth dress against her skin,
Was she not the one who wore it?
The anguish of six months,
Quite plainly, as it truly was,
Was she not the one who knew it?
Unable to twist her rein-like hair,
True anguish fallen upon her head,
Your sister-in-law could not stand still for crying.
Khan Manas was indeed a khan;
Then Semetey, born in his late years,
Was six months old.
